newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains on pound as British election polls narrow.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains on pound as British election polls narrow.

text.p: The dollar moved lower against most major currencies Wednesday but rose vs. the British pound as polls showed next week's elections in Britain could be much tighter than previously thought.
A poll by the British newspaper the Guardian showed the opposition Labour party leading the ruling Conservatives by only five percentage points, down from 14 a week ago.
The prospect of a weak government emerging from the polls suggested British officials would delay a much-anticipated interest rate hike. This triggered heavy sales of the pound.

"Sterling was sold rather aggressively since the New York opening. The possibility of a hung Parliament has really taken a lot of the luster out of the pound," said Stephen Flanagan, senior currency dealer at Credit Agricole.
The pound also suffered from a pair of reports showing Europe's proposed single currency, the euro, stands a good chance of launching as scheduled in 1999.
The European Commission in its semi-annual report predicted 13 of 15 potential participants would meet the budget deficit targets to qualify for monetary union.
Later, the International Monetary Fund urged Europe to press ahead with the euro and Deputy Research Director Flemming Larsen said the IMF was "very optimistic" it would launch on time.
With Britain not slated to join the euro group, many European investors sold the pound in favour of the dollar and European currencies.

"Sterling for some time has been a very successful currency. If people get more comfortable with the euro, you would expect sterling to lose some ground," said John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.
The pound fell to $1.6230 late Wednesday from $1.6333 in late Tuesday trade.
The dollar settled at 1.7135 German marks, down from 1.7172, and 126.05 Japanese yen, down from 126.32. The dollar dipped to 1.4625 Swiss francs from 1.4635 and Canadian $1.3939 from C$1.3953.
The dollar slipped vs. the yen in Asian trading after Bank of Japan Gov. Yasuo Matsushita said Japan's economic firmness was increasing, which could prompt inflation concerns.
Dealers said the comments sparked speculation on Japanese interest rate hikes, which would boost the yen.
But investors remained hesitant to aggressively trade the dollar against the yen as the weekend meeting of officials from the Group of Seven industrial nations draws near.
The risk of an official statement calling for the downtrodden yen to rise against the dollar kept market players sidelined.
"I don't think the G7 will say anything that will be bullish for the dollar," said Vincent Amaru, vice president and currency trader at Citibank.
Dealers also noted that Japanese officials have been unusually quiet as the dollar has edged toward its recent five-year high against the yen, making investors even more cautious.
"There's quite a bit of confusion, and perhaps that's their intent. When there is doubt, you can keep the market on its heels," said Flanagan.
